What does the Lake County Recorder do?

The Lake County Recorder records and preserves public land records, including deeds, mortgages, liens, releases, leases and subdivision plats. The office also takes articles of incorporation, assumed business names, military discharges and UCC filings.

It generally does not handle court orders, decrees, judgments, wills, marriage licenses or birth and death certificates. If you are selling a house that came through an estate, the court file and the recorded deed are kept in different places, so expect to visit both.

Records can be viewed or purchased at lcrecorder.com, and staff speak Spanish and use sign language, according to the county's page.

Where is the Lake County Recorder's office and when is it open?

The Recorder is on the second floor of Building A at 2293 N. Main Street in Crown Point, and it is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

What does Indiana law say about recording fees?

Indiana Code 36-2-7-10 sets the recorder's fee schedule. In the 2025 Justia copy, recording a deed or other instrument other than a mortgage costs $25, and a mortgage costs $55.

ServiceFee under IC 36-2-7-10
Deed or other instrument (not a mortgage)$25
Mortgage$55
Page larger than 8.5 by 14 inches$25 for the first page, $5 for each additional
Each added transaction on a release, partial release or assignment$7 on top of the $25 fee
Copy up to 11 by 17 inches$1 per page
Copy larger than 11 by 17 inches$5 per page
Acknowledging or certifying a document$5

Counties may add some charges by ordinance, such as an affordable housing fee of up to $10 per document. That Justia copy may not be current, and the statute requires the recorder to post the fee schedule, so confirm the total with the office or your title company before closing.

One more fee matters on tax-related releases. For a release of a political subdivision's lien on property sold or transferred under the tax sale and redevelopment statutes, the statute lists $25 per parcel for each subdivision with a lien.

What fees does Lake County add for online access and e-recording?

A Lake County ordinance sets a few charges tied to the Recorder. Searching the Recorder's website costs $3 per request, with $1 going to the vendor and $2 to the Recorder's Enhanced Access Fund. Printed pages from requested documents cost $1 each, and the ordinance also lists $3 for e-recording. Credit card charges vary by card company.

Because ordinances are amended often, ask the Recorder to confirm current amounts.

How does e-recording work in Lake County?

Lake County has accepted electronic recordings since March 2021, and the county says it receives over half of its documents that way. E-recording is open to title companies, law firms, banks and other businesses that regularly record land records.

The county says documents return in hours instead of days, and rejected documents can be fixed and resubmitted within hours. It lists four vendors:

  • Simplifile, which handles both transfer and non-transfer documents (1-800-460-5657)
  • Corporation Service Company, for non-transfer documents (1-866-652-0111)
  • Indecomm Global Services, for non-transfer documents (877-272-5250)
  • GOePN (888-325-3365, ext. 1)

A seller does not sign up for any of these. The title company or closing attorney does it.

What must a deed show before the Lake County Recorder will record it?

The instrument has to carry the name of the person who prepared it, in a legible printed, typed, stamped or signed form, such as "This instrument was prepared by" followed by a name. It also must state that the preparer took reasonable care to redact Social Security numbers, under penalty of perjury.

Before the deed goes to the County Auditor, the parties also complete a sales disclosure form. All parties to the conveyance sign it, and it goes first to the county assessor for review. The Auditor processes it after that and sends it on to the assessor, who keeps it for five years. Each parcel generally needs its own form.

The rule covers deeds and contracts of sale for value, and transfers by foreclosure, divorce, court order or probate. It excludes security instruments such as mortgages, short-term leases, utility easements and most quitclaim deeds. Questions about the Lake County Auditor's real estate desk go to 219-755-3157.

Is there a transfer tax when recording a deed in Lake County?

The documents we reviewed list recording fees, not a transfer tax. The recorder fee statute and the county Recorder page name recording and copy charges, and the county's Auditor real estate page was still a placeholder when we read it.

For a closing figure, call the Auditor at 219-755-3157 or the Recorder at 219-755-3730, or ask the title company for its settlement statement.

What is the story behind the Crown Point courthouse and the county seat?

Lake County was established in 1837 and Liverpool was its first seat. Lake Court House, later renamed Crown Point, was chosen as the seat in 1840. Solon Robinson and his family were the first settlers in the Crown Point area, arriving on October 31, 1834.

The Old Lake County Courthouse, nicknamed the Grand Old Lady, was begun in 1878 and expanded through 1928. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974, and a new Government Center opened the next year. Crown Point had 33,899 residents in 2020.

The Recorder's page lists one office, at 2293 N. Main Street. Lake County covers 626.5 square miles and has 19 incorporated cities and towns, so that office serves places as different as Gary, Hammond and Crown Point.

How do delinquent taxes show up when recording a Lake County sale?

Unpaid property tax is a claim against the parcel, so a title search will turn it up before a deed is recorded. Lake County's 2026 tax sale began online on September 4, 2026, and redemption for certificates sold expires September 8, 2027.

A cash buyer works around these items the same way a title company does. Back taxes, liens and open mortgages are paid from the proceeds, releases are recorded, and the deed follows. The released liens are separate recordings with their own fees.

  • Gather the deed, the tax bill and any lien or mortgage payoff letters
  • Confirm the legal description and the parcel number
  • Sign the sales disclosure form and the deed at the title company
  • Let the title company record the deed and releases through a vendor or at the Recorder
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Why do older Lake County properties need extra title attention?

Industry built much of the county. U.S. Steel founded Gary Works in 1906, and the county's population peaked at 546,253 in 1970 before falling to 498,700 in 2020. Gary's 2020 census counted 23.2% of its housing units as vacant.

Houses that have changed hands through estates, tax sales or long vacancies can carry old liens or unrecorded releases. Ask the title company to run the chain of title early so any missing release can be recorded before the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Lake County, Indiana?

Deeds are recorded with the Lake County Recorder at 2293 N. Main Street, Building A, 2nd Floor in Crown Point. Title companies usually send them electronically.

How much does the Lake County Recorder charge to record a deed?

Indiana Code lists $25 to record a deed or other instrument, and $55 for a mortgage. The county may add charges by ordinance, so ask the office for the current total.

Can I e-record in Lake County?

Yes, through approved vendors, but the service is open to businesses that regularly record land records, such as title companies and banks. Individuals normally use their closing agent.

What is a sales disclosure form in Indiana?

It is a form that every party to a covered conveyance signs before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The assessor reviews it first.

Who do I call at the Lake County Recorder?

Call 219-755-3730 on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. The fax number is (219) 648-6028.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Marion County?

Where is the Marion County Recorder's Office and when can you reach it?

The Marion County Recorder's Office is in the City-County Building at 200 E. Washington Street, Suite T-741, Indianapolis, IN 46204. The counter is open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday, and the main number is 317.327.4020.

Phone calls are answered from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, and messages are returned within one to two business days. The office says email to recorder@indy.gov gets the fastest response.

The office keeps permanent public records of property transactions, including deeds, liens, mortgages, easements and survey maps. Its page describes more than 11 million records in its care.

One change affects anyone who used to pick up a blank form there. Effective September 29, 2026, the office no longer provides forms or documents for recording. The stated reason is protecting owners from property fraud.

How do you record a deed in Marion County?

You record a deed in Marion County by first getting it stamped at the Assessor's Office, then submitting it to the Recorder with the fee. The county lists the steps on its Record Your Deed page.

  1. Gather the exact name of the current owner and the legal description. The Assessor's property report card or the current tax bill can supply them.
  2. Prepare the deed. The grantor is the person now on title and the grantee is the person who will be listed as the new owner. The county recommends an attorney.
  3. Sign and notarize the document.
  4. Take or mail it to the Assessor for the transfer stamp, with a separate check or money order for each office.
  5. The Recorder records it and returns it to you.
  6. Apply for any deductions you qualify for through the Marion County Auditor.

Documents can be submitted by mail, through e-recording partners or in person. Marion County has leaned heavily on electronic filing. In November 2025 the office recorded 8,764 documents, and 7,948 of them came in as e-recordings.

What does it cost to record a deed in Marion County?

The county's deed page lists $35.00 per document at the Recorder, plus $10.00 per parcel per document and $20.00 for each sales disclosure at the Assessor. Those are separate offices, so they are paid separately.

ChargeAmountWhere
Recording fee for a deed$35.00 per documentRecorder
Transfer fee$10.00 per parcel per documentAssessor
Sales disclosure form$20.00 per form, if requiredAssessor
Copies of recorded documents$1 per page up to 11 by 17 inches (state schedule)Recorder

The state schedule in Indiana Code 36-2-7-10 sets a base fee of $25 for a deed and $55 for a mortgage. For a county with a consolidated city, the statute and the State Board of Accounts recorder manual describe extra pieces: an optional housing trust fee of $2.50 for the first page and $1 for each added page, an identification security fee of $2, and an optional affordable housing fee of up to $10. The county's published $35 figure is the number to plan around, and the Recorder's fee schedule governs if your document has extra pages or unusual features.

Oversized pages cost more under the state schedule, $25 for the first and $5 for each additional. Military discharge papers are recorded free of charge, per the county.

What must a Marion County deed include to be accepted?

A deed has to be notarized, carry specific statements and meet formatting rules, or the office will reject it. The county's requirements page cites Indiana Code for each point.

  • Notarization under IC 32-21-2-3.
  • A statement under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, plus the name of the person who prepared the instrument (IC 36-2-11-15).
  • Names of signers and witnesses printed identically throughout and typed under each signature (IC 36-2-11-16).
  • Two-inch top and bottom margins on the first and last pages for the recording stamp. Without them, an extra page is added (IC 36-2-11-16.5).
  • A street address where tax statements should be mailed (IC 32-21-2-3).
  • For a power of attorney signing, the document number of the power of attorney with the signature.

The notary's name must match the commission, with the county of residence, the commission expiration date and the date of notarization. Seals for commissions issued or renewed after July 1, 2018 must also show the words "notary public," "State of Indiana," "seal," and the seven-digit commission number.

Re-recording a document means paying the original fee again and stating the reason at the top of the page. The office asks for a self-addressed stamped envelope with paper returns.

Is there a transfer tax or sales disclosure in Marion County?

The county page for the Assessor describes transfer and sales disclosure fees, not a percentage transfer tax. Marion County lists a $10 transfer fee per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form.

Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3, the parties must complete and sign a sales disclosure form before a conveyance document is filed with the county auditor. The county assessor reviews it for accuracy and completeness and, if it passes, approves it and returns it to a party for filing. Marion County asks filers to prepare the form in the Properly system at forms.properlytaxes.com, then print and sign it.

The Assessor's counter at Room W121 will not process documents after 4 p.m., and it accepts cash, checks for the exact amount and credit cards, with a small extra charge on cards. The Assessor cannot help prepare a deed, so use an attorney or title company.

How does the Recorder help protect owners from deed fraud?

Marion County offers a free Property Fraud Alert service for Marion County residents, promoted by the Recorder. Sign-up is at propertyfraudalert.com/INMARION.

The office reported 636 sign-ups in November 2025 and has put the alert on billboards. The same fraud concern is behind the 2026 change that ends the office's own blank forms.

For a seller this has a practical side. If you inherit a house or own one that sits empty, signing up is a free step worth taking.

Other services listed by the Recorder include a survivorship affidavit to remove a deceased owner from title, copies of deeds, a recording fee refund claim, and online search of real estate records.

What should a Marion County seller know about recording and closing?

Most sellers never record anything themselves, because the title or escrow company handles the stamp and the recording. The point of knowing the steps is to spot delays.

Delays usually come from one of these:

  • A missing notary detail or a name that differs from the vested deed.
  • A legal description that does not match the records.
  • A deed submitted without the Assessor stamp.
  • An unreleased mortgage or lien that still appears in the Recorder's index.

Marion County is the most populous of the Indiana counties covered in this guide, and its Recorder holds a large archive. Title work on an older house can reach back through many owners, which is why a clean chain of title is worth checking early. If you are weighing a quick sale of a house with title questions, a written offer from a cash buyer lets you see the terms before you commit.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Marion County, Indiana?

The county's Record Your Deed page lists $35.00 per document at the Recorder. The Assessor charges separately: $10.00 per parcel per document, and $20.00 for each sales disclosure when one is required.

Do I record a deed before or after the Assessor stamps it?

After. In Marion County the Assessor's transfer stamp is required before the Recorder can record the deed. Take the stamped deed to the Recorder in Room T-741.

Can I e-record a deed in Marion County?

Yes. The Recorder's Office accepts documents by mail, through its e-recording partners or in person. In November 2025, 7,948 of 8,764 recorded documents were e-recordings.

Does the Marion County Recorder still hand out deed forms?

No. The office says that from September 29, 2026 it no longer provides forms or documents for recording. Have an attorney or title company draft the deed.

What phone number and email reach the Marion County Recorder?

Call 317.327.4020 or email recorder@indy.gov. Calls are answered from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, and email is the fastest route according to the office.

Is there a percentage transfer tax in Marion County?

The official pages we read list flat fees only: $10 per parcel for the transfer and $20 per sales disclosure at the Assessor, plus the Recorder's fee. Ask your title company to confirm the total for your sale.

What does the Allen County Recorder do?

The recorder keeps the official public record of deeds and mortgages for Allen County, Indiana. When a house sells, the deed is recorded there so the new owner's title is on the public record.

Allen County is run by a seven-member County Council and a three-member Board of Commissioners. The recorder is one of several separately elected county officers, along with the auditor, treasurer, sheriff, coroner, surveyor and circuit court clerk. Most county offices moved in 1971 across Main Street from the courthouse to the Edwin J. Rousseau Centre in Fort Wayne.

The county treasurer's office is in the Rousseau Centre at 1 E Main St, Suite 104.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Allen County?

Indiana sets the base fee for recording a deed at $25, and a mortgage at $55. Those amounts come from Indiana Code 36-2-7-10, which applies to every county recorder.

ItemStatutory fee
Deed or other instrument (not a mortgage)$25
Mortgage$55
Oversized page (larger than 8.5 by 14 inches), first page$25
Oversized page, each additional page$5
Each added transaction on a release, partial release or assignment$7
Copy up to 11 by 17 inches$1 per page
Acknowledging or certifying a document$5
Releasing a political subdivision lien after a tax sale$25 per parcel

The statute also lets a county with an affordable housing fund add a $10 per document fee by ordinance. The version we read was a Justia copy, so confirm the current amounts with the recorder before you send a check.

What must a deed contain before the recorder accepts it?

An Indiana deed needs a preparer statement, an acknowledgment and a Social Security number affirmation. The checklist below comes from a county recording requirements sheet that applies Indiana law statewide.

  • The preparer must be identified on any instrument that needs a preparer statement.
  • The document must include an affirmation, under penalty of perjury, that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers unless the law requires them.
  • The affirmation goes at the end of the instrument, immediately before or after the preparer statement.
  • A grantee's mailing address that is not a street or rural route address needs a street or rural route address after it. A PO box does not meet the rule.
  • Each signer's name should be typed or printed under the signature exactly as signed.
  • A notarized document should show the notary's county of residence and commission expiration date.

Check each item against your deed draft before it goes to the recorder.

What is the sales disclosure form, and who files it?

The sales disclosure form goes to the county assessor first and to the county auditor second, and both steps come before the deed is filed. Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3 requires all parties to the conveyance to submit it, including exempt sellers and exempt buyers.

The assessor checks the form for accuracy and completeness. If it passes, the assessor stamps or approves it and returns it to one of the parties, who files it with the auditor.

The rule covers more than ordinary sales. A conveyance document includes transfers made through foreclosure, divorce, court order, condemnation and probate, along with partition documents. It excludes mortgages, trust deeds, leases shorter than 90 years and conveyances to the state or other governments, under IC 6-1.1-5.5-2.

What is the usual order of steps for an Allen County sale?

The deed is signed and notarized first, the sales disclosure form is approved next, and the recorder files the deed last. Here is a typical sequence under the Indiana rules above.

  1. The seller signs the deed in front of a notary, with the preparer statement and Social Security affirmation included.
  2. All parties sign the sales disclosure form.
  3. The county assessor reviews and stamps the form.
  4. The form and deed go to the county auditor.
  5. The recorder records the deed and charges the statutory fee.

When an inherited house is involved, the probate court order and the personal representative's deed have to line up with the names on the title. Check the existing record at the recorder before you list the house.

Where is Allen County, and how big is it?

Allen County is in northeast Indiana and is the largest county in the state by area, at 660.02 square miles. Fort Wayne is the county seat and the second-largest city in Indiana. It sits where the Maumee, St. Joseph and St. Marys rivers meet.

The county borders Noble, DeKalb, Adams, Wells, Huntington and Whitley counties in Indiana, and Defiance, Paulding and Van Wert counties in Ohio. It has 20 townships, and communities such as Grabill, Huntertown, Leo-Cedarville, Monroeville and Zanesville are within it.

Allen County was organized on December 17, 1823, from parts of Delaware and Randolph counties, and formally established on April 1, 1824 at the Ewing Tavern. Fort Wayne was chosen as the county seat in May 1824. The population reached 385,410 in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 402,329.

What is the Allen County Courthouse, and why does it matter for records?

The courthouse is a Beaux-Arts building completed in 1902 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 2003. Its cornerstone was laid in 1897, and the building cost $817,553.

The Allen County Genealogical Society publishes a free name index of deeds filed with the recorder, covering 1824 to 1903 and 1913 to 1999. If you inherited an older Fort Wayne house and need to understand an old transfer, that index can point you to the right deed.

The index is a finding aid. It does not replace a title search, and the page does not say whether the deed images are online.

What do sellers in Allen County usually face at the recorder?

Look for these items before you list. A release that covers several transactions costs an extra $7 for each transaction after the first.

  • A deed prepared with the wrong legal description or a misspelled name.
  • An inherited house where the title still shows a deceased owner.
  • A prior tax sale lien that has to be released, which carries a $25 fee per parcel.
  • A missing sales disclosure approval at the assessor or auditor.

The county's economy is varied. Allen County companies include Parkview Health, Lincoln Financial, Steel Dynamics, Franklin Electric, Do it Best and Sweetwater Sound, and there are four public school districts: East Allen, Fort Wayne Community Schools, Northwest Allen and Southwest Allen.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Allen County, Indiana?

The statutory fee is $25 for a deed or other non-mortgage instrument and $55 for a mortgage, under Indiana Code 36-2-7-10. Oversized pages and extra transactions cost more. Confirm current amounts with the recorder.

What does an Indiana deed need besides signatures?

It needs an acknowledgment, a preparer statement and an affirmation that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers. The grantee address must be a street or rural route address rather than a PO box, and a notary should list a county of residence and commission expiration.

What is the sales disclosure form in Indiana?

It is a form signed by all parties to a conveyance. The county assessor reviews and stamps it, and a party then files it with the county auditor before the deed is filed.

Where does the Allen County Treasurer sit?

The treasurer is in the Rousseau Centre at 1 E Main St, Suite 104, Fort Wayne, and the office hours listed in a 2025 notice were 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays. The recorder is a separate office.

Can I sell an inherited Allen County house without recording anything first?

The deed that transfers the house has to be recorded after the sale, and any prior transfer that left the title in a deceased owner's name may need to be put in order first. We buy Allen County houses as-is and can work with the title company on that.
